Q1Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterThermodynamics high confidence
why this chapterV proportional to T through the origin is an isobaric process, and the answer W/Q = nR dT / (nCp dT) = 2/5 for a monatomic gas rests on the first law with Cp = 5R/2.
subtopic 1Isobaric Process
why this subtopicThe V-T graph is a straight line through the origin, so A to B is isobaric and the answer is W/Q = nR dT / (n Cp dT) = R/Cp = 2/5 for a monatomic gas.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
The volume (V) of a monatomic gas varies with its temperature (T), as shown in the graph. The ratio of work done by the gas, to the heat absorbed by it, when it undergoes a change from state A to state B, is
  1. 13
  2. 23
  3. 25
  4. 27
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)
  1. Given process is isobaric
  2. dQ = n Cp dT
  3. dQ = n(52R)dT
  4. dW = P dV = n RdT
  5. Required ratio = dWdQ = nRdTn(52R)dT = 25

→ the working concludes: option 3

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
  1. The graph is a straight line through the origin, so V ∝ T, which means P is constant (isobaric process).
  2. Work done at constant pressure: W = P Δ V = nR Δ T.
  3. Heat absorbed at constant pressure: Q = nCp Δ T = 52 nR Δ T for a monatomic gas.
  4. WQ = nR Δ T52 nR Δ T = 25, which is option 3.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
33 highagree
difficultymedium · 3 steps
stepsRead the V-T graph as a straight line through the origin, so V is proportional to T and the process A to B is isobaric → Write the work done in an isobaric process as W = P dV = nR dT and the heat absorbed as Q = n Cp dT → Substitute Cp = 5R/2 for a monatomic gas and take the ratio W/Q = R/Cp
whyThe work is identifying the process as isobaric from the graph, then writing W and Q for that process and substituting the monatomic Cp to form the ratio.

AsksCalculationcalculateput numbers in and get a number out
ConceptA straight V-T line through the origin is a constant-pressure process, where W = nRΔ T and the heat supplied is nCpΔ T with Cp = 52R for a monatomic gas
Why this answerThis question requires a ratio computed for the process the graph shows, demonstrated by the stem's 'monatomic gas' with V plotted as a straight line through the origin against T.
NoteThe figure supplies one premise -- that V is proportional to T, hence constant pressure -- but the answer is produced by the heat-capacity arithmetic, so asks is calculate rather than read_diagram.
What catches a student
The trapoption 2Formula misusedformula_misusedthe right formula with a wrong power, a dropped term or the wrong quantity

Putting the internal energy change in place of the heat absorbed -- Cv = 32R where the process needs Cp = 52R -- turns the ratio into nRΔ T32nRΔ T = 23.

Who fallsa student who stores 32R as the heat capacity belonging to a monatomic gas and uses it wherever a monatomic gas is mentioned

Why it feels right23 is built from the two numbers the chapter attaches to a monatomic gas, R and 32R, so it looks like the answer the data was meant to give

  1. okV rises in proportion to T through the origin, so the pressure is constant and W = nRΔ T.
  2. badThe heat absorbed is the internal energy change, 32nRΔ T, so the ratio is 23.At constant pressure the gas warms and expands, so the heat supplied is nCpΔ T with Cp = 52R; Δ U is only the part of it that stays in the gas.
Also pullsoption 4

Who fallsa student who reaches for Cp = 72R, the value drilled on diatomic-gas problems

Why it feels rightthe structure R/Cp is right and 72R is the Cp that appears most often in worked examples

  1. okAt constant pressure the ratio of work to heat is R/Cp.
  2. badCp is 72R, so the ratio is 27.The stem says monatomic, so Cp = 52R; 72R belongs to a diatomic gas.
No route to itoption 1

back-solved the ratio: R/C = 13 needs a molar heat capacity of 3R, and the capacities in play for this process are 32R and 52R for a monatomic gas and 52R and 72R for a diatomic one, which give 23, 25 and 27 but never 13.

Q2Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterWaves high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on the harmonic frequencies of open (v/2L) and closed (nv/4L) organ pipes, which is taught in Waves.
subtopic 1Organ Pipe
why this subtopicThe answer depends on the harmonic frequencies of open (v/2L) and closed (nv/4L, odd n) organ pipes, equating the open pipe's fundamental to the closed pipe's third harmonic to get L = 80/6 cm.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
The fundamental frequency in an open organ pipe is equal to the third harmonic of a closed organ pipe. If the length of the closed organ pipe is 20 cm, the length of the open organ pipe is
  1. 12.5 cm
  2. 8 cm
  3. 13.2 cm
  4. 16 cm
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)
  1. For closed organ pipe, third harmonic
  2. = 3v4l
  3. For open organ pipe, fundamental frequency
  4. = v2l'
  5. Given,
  6. 3v4l = v2l'
  7. ⇒ l' = 4l3 × 2 = 2l3
  8. = 2 × 203 = 13.33 cm

→ the working concludes: option 3

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · medium
  1. Fundamental of the open pipe: fo = v2L'.
  2. Third harmonic of the closed pipe: f3 = 3v4L.
  3. Set them equal: v2L' = 3v4L ⇒ L' = 4L6 = 2L3.
  4. L' = 2 × 20 cm3 = 13.33 cm, closest to option 3 (13.2 cm).
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
33 mediumagree
difficultymedium · 3 steps
stepsRecall the fundamental frequency of an open pipe of length L': f = v/(2L') → Recall that a closed pipe has only odd harmonics, so its third harmonic is 3v/(4L) with L = 20 cm → Equate the two expressions, cancel v and solve for L'
whyTwo standard pipe-resonance formulas must be recalled and equated, then a one-line ratio solved for the open-pipe length; no insight beyond the formulas is needed.
the catchA distractor equals the exact result of misreading 'third harmonic' of a closed pipe as its third mode / second overtone (n = 5, 5v/4L), a common confusion since closed pipes have only odd harmonics.

Categories
TypeMCQmcqa question and four answers, nothing lettered or listed
AsksCalculationcalculateput numbers in and get a number out
ConceptA closed pipe sounds only odd harmonics, so its third harmonic is 3v/4L -- three times its fundamental -- and not the third frequency up the ladder
Why this answerThis question requires a length computed by equating two pipe frequencies, demonstrated by 'the fundamental frequency in an open organ pipe is equal to the third harmonic of a closed organ pipe' with the closed length printed as 20 cm.
NoteTwo-thirds of 20 cm is 13.3 cm and option 3 prints 13.2 cm; the key is (3) and the tag follows it, with the rounding recorded here rather than treated as a second answer.
What catches a student
The trapoption 2Formula misusedformula_misusedthe right formula with a wrong power, a dropped term or the wrong quantity

Counting 'third' along the frequencies a closed pipe can actually sound -- v/4L, 3v/4L, 5v/4L -- lands on 5v/4L, and equating that with v/2Lopen gives Lopen = 2(20)/5 = 8 cm instead of 2(20)/3 = 13.3 cm.

Who fallsa student who knows a closed pipe omits the even harmonics and therefore counts the third item in its list of permitted modes

Why it feels rightthe counting is careful and uses the right physics -- only odd modes exist -- so the third one up really does look like the third harmonic

  1. okA closed pipe can sound only v/4L, 3v/4L, 5v/4L, and the open pipe's fundamental is v/2L.
  2. badThe third of those frequencies is 5v/4L, so set v/2Lopen = 5v/(4×20) and get 8 cm.The harmonic number is the multiple of the fundamental, so the third harmonic is 3× v/4L; it is the first overtone of the closed pipe, not the third mode.
No route to itoption 1

solved for every length these two pipe formulas can produce: pairing the open fundamental (v/2L or, if the pipes are mixed up, v/4L) with a closed-pipe frequency (3v/4L, 5v/4L or a mistaken 3v/2L) gives 13.3, 8, 6.7 or 4 cm from the printed 20 cm, and 12.5 cm is not among them.

No route to itoption 4

the same enumeration rules this out: 16 cm needs Lopen = 0.8Lclosed, which no pairing of v/2L or v/4L with 3v/4L or 5v/4L produces, since those pairings only ever give two-thirds, two-fifths, one-third or one-fifth of the 20 cm.

subjectPhysics
chapterKinetic Theory of Gases high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on the kinetic-theory relation v_rms = sqrt(3k_BT/m), solved for the temperature at which v_rms equals the Earth's escape speed (11.2 km/s, used only as a given value).
subtopic 1RMS Speed and Its Dependence on Temperature

printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
At what temperature will the rms speed of oxygen molecules become just sufficient for escaping from the Earth's atmosphere? (Given : Mass of oxygen molecule (m) = 2.76 × 10-26 kg Boltzmann's constant kB = 1.38 × 10-23 JK-1)
  1. 5.016 × 104 K
  2. 8.360 × 104 K
  3. 2.508 × 104 K
  4. 1.254 × 104 K
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (2)
  1. Vescape = 11200 m/s
  2. Say at temperature T it attains Vescape
  3. So, 3kB TmO2 = 11200 m/s
  4. On solving,
  5. T = 8.360 × 104 K

→ the working concludes: option 2

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 2 · high
  1. For the molecules to escape, vrms = ve = 11.2 km s-1 = 1.12 × 104 m s-1.
  2. vrms = 3kBTm ⇒ T = m ve23kB.
  3. ve2 = (1.12 × 104)2 = 1.2544 × 108 m2 s-2.
  4. m ve2 = 2.76 × 10-26 × 1.2544 × 108 = 3.462 × 10-18 J.
  5. 3kB = 3 × 1.38 × 10-23 = 4.14 × 10-23 J K-1.
  6. T = 3.462 × 10-184.14 × 10-23 ≈ 8.36 × 104 K, which is option 2.

ConceptEscape needs vrms to reach the escape speed of 11.2 km/s, and 12mvrms2 = 32kBT fixes the temperature at mv2/3kB
Why this answerThis question requires a temperature computed from an energy balance, demonstrated by the stem supplying the molecular mass and Boltzmann's constant and asking at what temperature the rms speed suffices 'for escaping from the Earth's atmosphere'.
NoteThe escape speed of 11.2 km/s is not printed in the stem; the student has to supply it, which every route above assumes.
What catches a student
The trapoption 1Formula misusedformula_misusedthe right formula with a wrong power, a dropped term or the wrong quantity

Oxygen is diatomic, so a student who reaches for five degrees of freedom writes 12mv2 = 52kBT and gets T = mv2/5kB = 5.016×104 K; the rms speed is set by translation alone, which is 32kBT.

Who fallsa student who has learnt that a diatomic molecule has five degrees of freedom and applies that count to the speed as well as to the energy

Why it feels rightthe molecule in the stem really is diatomic, and the five-halves factor is the one used for its internal energy and its heat capacities

  1. okSet the kinetic energy of the molecule equal to its thermal energy and solve for T.
  2. badOxygen is diatomic, so the thermal energy is 52kBT and T = mv2/5kB.Only the three translational degrees carry the speed, so vrms comes from 32kBT; rotation stores energy but moves nothing through space.
Also pullsoption 4

Who fallsa student who writes the energy balance as 12mv2 = kBT, dropping the three-halves

Why it feels rightthe digits match what the calculator shows: mv2/2kB is 1.254×105, and 1.254 is printed on the page

  1. okPut v = 11.2 km/s and the given m and kB into an energy balance.
  2. bad12mv2 = kBT gives 1.254, and the option reading 1.254 must be it.Restore the three-halves -- 12mv2 = 32kBT gives 8.36×104 K -- and check the exponent as well as the digits, since this route's own value is 105, not 104.
No route to itoption 3

worked out what this value needs: 2.508×104 is the mantissa of mv2/kB = 2.5088×105, which requires the half AND the three-halves to be dropped together, and then the power of ten to be misread as well -- three departures, where option 4 needs one factor and one exponent; no single operation on the printed m, kB and 11.2 km/s reaches it.

subjectPhysics
chapterThermodynamics high confidence
why this chapterThe answer depends on the Carnot (ideal heat engine) efficiency formula 1 - T2/T1 = 1 - 273/373 = 26.8%, which is taught in Thermodynamics.
subtopic 1Carnot Engine
why this subtopicThe answer uses the ideal (Carnot) engine efficiency 1 - T2/T1 = 1 - 273/373 = 26.8%.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
The efficiency of an ideal heat engine working between the freezing point and boiling point of water, is
  1. 6.25%
  2. 20%
  3. 26.8%
  4. 12.5%
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)
  1. Efficiency of ideal heat engine, η = (1 - T2T1)
  2. T2 : Sink temperature
  3. T1 : Source temperature
  4. %η = (1 - T2T1) × 100
  5. = (1 - 273373) × 100
  6. = (100373) × 100 = 26.8%

→ the working concludes: option 3

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
  1. An ideal (Carnot) engine has efficiency η = 1 - TcTh.
  2. Freezing point Tc = 273 K, boiling point Th = 373 K.
  3. η = 1 - 273373 = 100373 ≈ 0.268.
  4. η ≈ 26.8%, which is option 3.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
33 highagree
difficultymedium · 2 steps
stepsrecognise the ideal engine as a Carnot engine and convert the reservoir temperatures 0 C and 100 C to kelvin (273 K and 373 K) → substitute into the Carnot efficiency 1 - T_cold/T_hot and evaluate 100/373 as a percentage
whyThe work is a Celsius-to-kelvin conversion of both reservoir temperatures followed by one substitution into the Carnot efficiency formula and a non-round division.
page 2 · printed answer 3 · open source PDF at this page · NEET_2018_Code_AA_official.pdf
Categories
TypeMCQmcqa question and four answers, nothing lettered or listed
AsksCalculationcalculateput numbers in and get a number out
ConceptCarnot efficiency is 1 - TC/TH with both temperatures in kelvin, so water's freezing and boiling points mean 273 K and 373 K
Why this answerThis question requires a Carnot efficiency computed from two reservoir temperatures, demonstrated by 'an ideal heat engine working between the freezing point and boiling point of water'.
Noteno_trap is a finding here, not a gap: the Celsius error that this question is usually built to catch gives 100 per cent, which the paper does not print, so the three wrong options are a numerical spread rather than routes.
What catches a student
The trapNo trapno_trapnothing pulls; the other options are only filler

The one wrong move this stem invites is putting 0 and 100 degrees Celsius into 1 - TC/TH, which yields 100 per cent, and that is not printed. Each wrong option was then back-solved for the temperature pair it would need: 6.25 per cent needs 273 K against 291 K, 20 per cent needs 273 K against 341 K, 12.5 per cent needs 273 K against 312 K, and no reading of the freezing and boiling points -- Celsius, kelvin, Fahrenheit or Rankine, the last two giving 84.9 and 26.8 per cent -- produces any of those pairs.

No route to itoption 2

20 per cent requires TC/TH = 0.8, that is 273 K with a source at 341 K or 373 K with a sink at 298 K; neither number is obtainable from the two temperatures printed, and inverting the formula to 1 - TH/TC gives a negative efficiency rather than this one.

No route to itoption 4

12.5 per cent requires TC/TH = 0.875, which from 373 K needs a sink at 326 K; the printed reservoirs differ by 100 K in 373 K, so no pairing of the stem's two temperatures, in any scale, yields one eighth.

No route to itoption 1

6.25 per cent requires the two reservoirs to differ by one sixteenth of the hotter one, about 18 K; the stem's reservoirs differ by 100 K, and halving or doubling the correct 26.8 per cent does not reach it either, so the value only widens the spread.

Q6Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterCurrent Electricity high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on series and parallel combination of resistors with a cell's internal resistance (I = E/(R_eq + r)), which is taught in Current Electricity.
subtopic 1Combination of Resistors
subtopic 2Relationship Between EMF, Potential Difference and Current With Internal Resistance
why this subtopicThe answer n = 10 comes from the series (nR) and parallel (R/n) equivalent resistances placed in I = E/(R_eq + r) with internal resistance r = R, giving a current ratio of n.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
A set of 'n' equal resistors, of value 'R' each, are connected in series to a battery of emf 'E' and internal resistance 'R'. The current drawn is I. Now, the 'n' resistors are connected in parallel to the same battery. Then the current drawn from battery becomes 10 I. The value of 'n' is
  1. 20
  2. 11
  3. 10
  4. 9
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)
  1. I = EnR + R ...(i)
  2. 10 I = ERn + R ...(ii)
  3. Dividing (ii) by (i),
  4. 10 = (n + 1)R(1n + 1)R
  5. After solving the equation, n = 10

→ the working concludes: option 3

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
  1. In series the external resistance is nR, so I = EnR + R = E(n+1)R.
  2. In parallel the external resistance is Rn, so 10I = ERn + R = nE(n+1)R.
  3. Dividing: 10II = nE/((n+1)R)E/((n+1)R) = n.
  4. n = 10, which is option 3.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
33 highagree
difficultymedium · 3 steps
stepsWrite the series-case current: equivalent resistance nR plus internal resistance R, so I = E/((n+1)R) → Write the parallel-case current: equivalent resistance R/n plus internal resistance R, so current = nE/((n+1)R) → Take the ratio of the two currents, set it equal to 10, and solve for n
whyThe work is two equivalent-resistance-with-internal-resistance current expressions followed by one ratio that simplifies to a single linear equation in n.

Who fallsa student who writes the series resistance as nR because the n resistors are what the stem lists, and keeps the internal resistance only where the parallel combination made them think of it

subjectPhysics

Q8Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterWave Optics high confidence

publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
Unpolarised light is incident from air on a plane surface of a material of refractive index 'μ'. At a particular angle of incidence 'i', it is found that the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular to each other. Which of the following options is correct for this situation?
  1. i=sin-1(1μ)
  2. Reflected light is polarised with its electric vector perpendicular to the plane of incidence
  3. Reflected light is polarised with its electric vector parallel to the plane of incidence
  4. i=tan-1(1μ)
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (2)
  1. When reflected light rays and refracted rays are perpendicular, reflected light is polarised with electric field vector perpendicular to the plane of incidence.
  2. Also, tan i = μ (Brewster angle)

→ the working concludes: option 2

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 2 · high
  1. Reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular, so i + r = 90°, i.e. r = 90° - i.
  2. Snell's law: sin i = μ sin r = μ cos i, so tan i = μ, i.e. i = tan-1μ (Brewster's angle); options 1 and 4 are wrong.
  3. At Brewster's angle the component with →E in the plane of incidence is not reflected, so the reflected light is polarised with →E perpendicular to the plane of incidence, which is option 2.

whyThe work is identifying the Brewster condition from the perpendicular-rays clue, then applying two separate recalls: the tan i = μ relation and the direction of the electric vector in the reflected polarised light.

An electron of mass m with an initial velocity →V = V0ˆı (V0 > 0) enters an electric field →E = -E0ˆı (E0 = constant > 0) at t = 0. If λ0 is its de-Broglie wavelength initially, then its de-Broglie wavelength at time t is

  2. λ0 = hmV0    ...(i)
  3. Acceleration of electron
  4. a = eE0m
  5. Velocity after time 't'
  6. V = (V0 + eE0mt)
  7. So, λ = hmV = hm(V0 + eE0mt)
  8. = hmV0[1 + eE0mV0t] = λ0[1 + eE0mV0t]    ...(ii)

  3. Velocity at time t: v = V0 + eE0mt = V0(1 + eE0mV0t).
  4. De-Broglie wavelength: λ = hmv = hmV0(1 + eE0mV0t).

A toy car with charge q moves on a frictionless horizontal plane surface under the influence of a uniform electric field →E. Due to the force q→E, its velocity increases from 0 to 6 m/s in one second duration. At that instant the direction of the field is reversed. The car continues to move for two more seconds under the influence of this field. The average velocity and the average speed of the toy car between 0 to 3 seconds are respectively
  1. 1 m/s, 3.5 m/s
  2. 1 m/s, 3 m/s
  3. 2 m/s, 4 m/s
  4. 1.5 m/s, 3 m/s
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (2)
  1. Acceleration a = 6-01 = 6 ms-2
  2. For t = 0 to t = 1 s,
  3. S1 = 12× 6(1)2 = 3 m ...(i)
  4. For t = 1 s to t = 2 s,
  5. S2 = 6.1 - 12× 6(1)2 = 3 m ...(ii)
  6. For t = 2 s to t = 3 s,
  7. S3 = 0 - 12× 6(1)2 = -3 m ...(iii)
  8. Total displacement S = S1 + S2 + S3 = 3 m
  9. Average velocity = 33 = 1 ms-1
  10. Total distance travelled = 9 m
  11. Average speed = 93 = 3 ms-1

→ the working concludes: option 2

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 2 · high
  1. Acceleration magnitude: a = 6-01 = 6 m/s2.
  2. From 0 to 1 s: s1 = 12(6)(1)2 = 3 m forward.
  3. After reversal the car decelerates at 6 m/s2, so it stops at t = 2 s: s2 = 6(1) - 12(6)(1)2 = 3 m forward.
  4. From 2 to 3 s it accelerates backward from rest: s3 = 12(6)(1)2 = 3 m backward.
  5. Net displacement = 3 + 3 - 3 = 3 m; total distance = 3 + 3 + 3 = 9 m.
  6. Average velocity = 33 = 1 m/s; average speed = 93 = 3 m/s, which is option 2.

A block of mass m is placed on a smooth inclined wedge ABC of inclination θ as shown in the figure. The wedge is given an acceleration 'a' towards the right. The relation between a and θ for the block to remain stationary on the wedge is

  2. a = gsinθ

  1. In non-inertial frame,
  2. Nsinθ = ma ...(i)

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. The incline is smooth, so the only forces on the block are its weight mg (down) and the normal reaction N, perpendicular to face AB, pointing up and to the right.

  3. Vertically there is no acceleration, so Ncosθ = mg.
  4. Dividing the two equations gives tanθ = ag, so a = gtanθ, which is option 4.

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
  1. Each option is an arenium ion (sigma complex) with the sp3 carbon C1 bearing H and Y; the + charge is delocalised over C2, C4 and C6 (ortho and para to C1).
  2. NO2 is strongly electron-withdrawing (-I, -R), so a resonance form with + on the carbon bearing NO2 is strongly destabilising.
  3. Option 1: NO2 is on C5 (meta to C1), which never carries the + charge.
  4. Options 2 and 3: NO2 is on C4 (para), and option 4: NO2 is on C2 (ortho); in each a resonance form places + on C–NO2.
  5. Hence option 1 is the most stable carbocation.

The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
  1. +1HBrO ⟶ 0Br2, E°HBrO/Br2 = 1.595 V
  2. +1HBrO ⟶ +5BrO3-, E°BrO3-/HBrO = 1.5 V
  3. E°cell for the disproportionation of HBrO,
  4. E°cell = E°HBrO/Br2 - E°BrO3-/HBrO

  1. A species disproportionates if E°cell = E°(its reduction) - E°(reduction of the higher state to it) > 0.
  2. For HBrO: E°cell = E°HBrO/Br2 - E°BrO3-/HBrO = 1.595 - 1.5 = +0.095 V > 0, spontaneous.
  3. For Br2: E°cell = 1.0652 - 1.595 = -0.53 V < 0, not spontaneous.
  4. For BrO3-: E°cell = 1.5 - 1.82 = -0.32 V < 0, not spontaneous.

For the redox reaction
MnO4- + C2O42- + H+ ⟶ Mn2+ + CO2 + H2O
The correct coefficients of the reactants for the balanced equation are
MnO4-     C2O42-     H+
  1. 2     16     5
  2. 2     5     16
  3. 16     5     2
  4. 5     16     2
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (2)
  1. n-factor of MnO4- ⇒ 5
  2. n-factor of C2O42- ⇒ 2
  3. Ratio of n-factors of MnO4- and C2O42- is 5 : 2
  4. So, molar ratio in balanced reaction is 2 : 5
  5. ∴ The balanced equation is
  6. 2MnO4- + 5C2O42- + 16H+ → 2Mn2+ + 10CO2 + 8H2O

→ the working concludes: option 2

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 2 · high
  1. In MnO4-, Mn goes from +7 to +2 in Mn2+: a gain of 5e- per Mn.
  2. In C2O42-, each C goes from +3 to +4 in CO2: a loss of 2e- per oxalate ion.
  3. Equate electrons (LCM 10): 2 MnO4- + 5 C2O42- → 2 Mn2+ + 10 CO2.
  4. Balance O with water: LHS has 8 + 20 = 28 O, CO2 has 20, so 8 H2O on the right.
  5. Balance H: 8 H2O needs 16 H+; charge check: -2 - 10 + 16 = +4 = 2(+2).
  6. Coefficients 2, 5, 16 for MnO4-, C2O42-, H+, which is option 2.

Which one of the following conditions will favour maximum formation of the product in the reaction, A2(g) + B2(g) ⇌ X2(g) Δr H = -X kJ?
  1. High temperature and high pressure
  2. Low temperature and low pressure
  3. Low temperature and high pressure
  4. High temperature and low pressure
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)
  1. A2(g) + B2(g) ⇌ X2(g); Δ H = -x kJ
  2. On increasing pressure equilibrium shifts in a direction where pressure decreases i.e. forward direction.
  3. On decreasing temperature, equilibrium shifts in exothermic direction i.e., forward direction.
  4. So, high pressure and low temperature favours maximum formation of product.

→ the working concludes: option 3

Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
  1. Δr H = -X kJ < 0, so the forward reaction is exothermic and lowering temperature shifts equilibrium towards X2.
  2. Δ ng = 1 - (1+1) = -1, so increasing pressure shifts equilibrium towards fewer gas moles, i.e. towards X2.
  3. Low temperature and high pressure is option 3.

Who fallsa student who has learnt both terms from the same paragraph and keeps them as a pair with no hook for which is which

Why it feels rightthe stem's word is 'similarity', and analogy is the word that itself means being alike

  1. okThe forelimbs of these vertebrates resemble one another in their bones.
  2. badA resemblance between organs is analogy.Analogy is a shared function reached from different structures; one bone plan put to different uses is homology.
Also pullsoption 1

Who fallsa student who has learnt convergent evolution as the process that makes unrelated animals come to look alike

Why it feels rightthe stem reports a similarity, and convergence is the process whose stated outcome is similarity

  1. okConvergent evolution makes animals of different ancestry come to resemble each other.
  2. badSo a similarity of forelimb bones is convergent evolution.Convergence gives analogous organs such as the wings of an insect and a bird; a shared bone plan comes from a common ancestor, which is divergence.
Also pullsoption 4

Who fallsa student who has learnt adaptive radiation as one ancestral stock diverging into many forms

Why it feels rightthe forelimb example is about one plan diverging from a common ancestor, which is the sentence adaptive radiation is taught with

  1. okMany vertebrates carrying one bone plan descend from a common ancestor whose descendants took up different ways of life.
  2. badThat is adaptive radiation.Adaptive radiation names the process of one stock diversifying in a place, as with Darwin's finches; the shared structure itself is called homology.

  1. ABO blood group is controlled by gene I with three alleles IA, IB, i, so it shows multiple alleles (c); IA and IB are dominant over i (a); IA IB expresses both A and B, so it shows co-dominance (b). Incomplete dominance and polygenic inheritance do not apply, so a, b and c is option 2.

stepsRecall the ABO blood-group gene I with its three alleles IA, IB and i (multiple alleles) → Recall the allele relationships: IA and IB are co-dominant, while IA and IB are each dominant over the recessive i, so plain dominance also applies → Reject incomplete dominance and polygenic inheritance, then match the accepted set of statements to the option combinations
whyThe work is recalling the ABO allele system and testing each of five inheritance patterns against it, including spotting that IA/IB over i is ordinary dominance, before matching the set to an option.
the catchThe chapter stresses ABO as the example of co-dominance and multiple alleles, so 'Dominance' (IA/IB over i) is easy to drop, and the options that pair co-dominance with polygenic or incomplete dominance catch candidates who mix up the blood-group example with other inheritance patterns.

TypeStatementsstatementslettered statements, the answer is which combination is right
AsksStated factfact_linea fact NCERT states: what, who or where
ConceptABO blood grouping is one gene with three alleles: IA and IB are co-dominant with each other and both dominant over i, so dominance, co-dominance and multiple alleles all show in the same system, with no blending and no second gene
Why this answerThis question requires each named inheritance pattern to be checked against what is stated about the ABO gene, demonstrated by polygenic inheritance (e) standing in three of the four options while only 'a, b and c' leaves it out.
Notehalf_right was taken over nearby_fact because every wrong option is a set of three items of which two hold and one fails — (e) in options 3 and 4, (d) in option 1 — which is what that label is for.
What catches a student
The trapoption 3Partly correcthalf_rightone part of the option is right and one part is wrong

Option 3 keeps the two facts the ABO section is remembered for, co-dominance and multiple alleles, and fills its third slot with polygenic inheritance, reached by reading 'three alleles of one gene' as 'more than one gene'.

Who fallsa student who has learnt ABO as the textbook case of multiple alleles and co-dominance and has not asked whether plain dominance is also shown there

Why it feels rightits first two items are exactly what the ABO section is remembered for, and 'multiple allele' and 'polygenic' both say more than one

  1. okABO shows co-dominance, since IA and IB each express their own sugar, and multiple alleles, since one gene carries three.
  2. badIf those two alleles are co-dominant then nothing is dominant, so item (a) is out.The third allele i is recessive to both IA and IB, so dominance is shown in the very same system.
  3. badThree alleles at work means more than one factor, so polygenic inheritance is in.Polygenic means several genes each adding a little, as in human skin colour; ABO is a single gene.
Also pullsoption 1

Who fallsa student who reads the AB phenotype as a blend of A and B

Why it feels right(b) and (d) are the two items whose names differ by one word, and a group that is 'both at once' looks like an intermediate

  1. okAn AB individual does express something from each allele.
  2. badThat intermediate condition is incomplete dominance, so (d) belongs alongside (b).In incomplete dominance the hybrid shows a third, intermediate phenotype, as the pink Snapdragon does; AB shows both sugars in full, which is co-dominance, so (d) stays out.
Also pullsoption 4

Who fallsa student who holds (a) and (c) securely and takes the third item from the same 'more than one' idea

Why it feels rightdominance and multiple alleles are both plainly true of ABO, so only the third item is in doubt, and polygenic inheritance also speaks of many

  1. okIA and IB are each dominant over i, and the gene has three alleles.
  2. badThree alleles means several contributors, which is polygenic inheritance.Count genes, not alleles: ABO is one gene, and what this option drops — co-dominance, item (b) — is what the AB phenotype shows.
